title: Pace of life and segregation: Europe versus New York
summary: On returning he felt a faster pace and segregation like a blocked bloodstream, compared with Europe's mingling of cultures.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: So when you got back, it looked a little peculiar.
But you'd been in Europe three years. There had been quite a few changes in music here, hadn't there. What did
you notice in that respect when you got back?

Yeah, the pace of life was much more... So that you're dealing... Over in Europe you're dealing with people...who have all got different things. You mingle more with cultures over there. But here you're segregated, there's segregation involved. You feel it in the air. You feel it in the tempo of the people. Over there you didn't feel it. Well, you'd feel it, but not as much as...
But that also has to do with pace.

It has a lot to do with pace. To me it's just like the blood running through your bloodstream, then, is blocked by an appendix or something. It was noticeable, you know, the (?) from here, there, and back again. You can see the way people answer, their motions, the way they jump(?) a thing. You know, it's more of a startling thing going on. I don't think they realize what they...

Well, it's always little things when you generalize like that. But it seems to me that from my experience coming here, that it's primarily New York. Because when I've been to cities like Pittsburgh and Chicago...
Now, wait a minute. I'm speaking about how many years ago. Forty, fifty, sixty...
Forty years ago. There's a big difference.
